catalog_quote: For determining stress in Ki-Luguru it is better to use the mora rather than the syllable as the basic unit. This seems to be the best way of accounting for stress patterns involving nasal compounds: e.g. iŋowo /íŋowo/ = banana but iŋombe /iŋómbe/ = cow iŋamo /íŋamo/ = filter but iŋanda /iŋánda/ = house Since this is a regular phenomenon in Ki-Luguru it is appropriate to analyse each nasal in a cluster as one mora. This will enable us to make a simple general statement that stress is regularly placed on the third mora from the end of a word. In two-mora words stress will naturally fall on the first mora, but as soon as a prefix is added, stress is shifted one place backwards in order to conform to the general rule of 'third mora from the end' stress placement: e.g. /bíki/ (tree); /túnda/ (fruit) but /líibiki/ in contrast with /liitúnda/ In suffixation too a shift in stress placement occurs only in order to conform to the general rule: e.g. Leka /léka/ : two-morae (=leave) Lek-ela /lékela/: no change of stress position Lek-el-eza (lekéleza): stress moves one step forward Lek-el-el-ela /lekeléela/: stress moves two steps forward. ... A full systematic account of stress placement in Ki-Luguru would deal also with secondary stress placement. However, since my intention here is to give only a sketch of some of the basic facts of Ki-Luguru, I will not attempt to deal with secondary stress placement.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the third mora counted from the end of the word. Morae: every vowel, each half of a long vowel, and every nasal in a nasal cluster (and a syllabic nasal) count as one mora. In syllable terms this gives antepenultimate stress in words of light syllables (/kólola/ 'he is looking', /íŋowo/ 'banana') and penultimate stress when the penult is heavy by a long vowel or a following nasal cluster (/kolóoka/ 'he is crossing', /iŋómbe/ 'cow', /iŋánda/ 'house'); the stress can even land on the nasal itself (/iŋ́amo/ 'filter'). Stress shifts rightward as suffixes are added (leka /léka/, lek-el-eza /lekéleza/, lek-el-el-ela /lekeléela/) and leftward when a prefix is added to a two-mora stem (/bikí/ 'tree' vs /líibiki/). Mkude also uses stress placement as the diagnostic for phonological vowel length (p. 39). A stressed vowel is 'normally slightly lengthened' (p. 41).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Acknowledged but not described: 'A full systematic account of stress placement in Ki-Luguru would deal also with secondary stress placement. However, since my intention here is to give only a sketch of some of the basic facts of Ki-Luguru, I will not attempt to deal with secondary stress placement.' (p. 47)
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as exceptions; the two-mora case (stress on the first mora, e.g. /léka/) is treated as the same rule. Tone: 'No clear evidence of lexical or grammatical tone has been detected in Ki-Luguru. Assuming that all Bantu languages were tonal at some earlier stage, we can only conclude that Ki-Luguru has lost that characteristic.' (p. 48). Corroborated first-hand by Petzell 2020: 121 ('no tonal contrast, either lexical or grammatical') and Petzell & Kühl 2017: 39.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('from the end of a word'); examples are citation-form nouns with class prefix and inflected verb forms (ka-o-lola 'he is looking'). Part III of the thesis separately treats sentence-level contrastive/nuclear stress and focus (pp. 273ff.), which is distinct from the word-stress rule. Author is a native speaker; p. 46 refers to 'my dialect' and the abbreviations distinguish Highland (HLK) and Lowland (LLK) Kiluguru.
new_statements.identity_note: Mkude 1974 describes Kiluguru as spoken by the author (a native speaker) and his consultant R. L. Jaka; he notes 'remarkable internal dialectal differences' (p. 7), distinguishes Highland Kiluguru (HLK) and Lowland Kiluguru (LLK) in his abbreviations, and flags one nasal-assimilation rule as 'obligatory in my dialect' (p. 46). No separate Glottolog dialect code applies; the description is language-level lugu1238 (ISO ruf). Seidel 1898 calls the language Ki-Ruguru (Uluguru mountains), same variety.
